_comment: Every metric must have: description (what it is), detects (what signal it catches), purpose (why it matters for trading), usage (how to read it), crossMetrics (how it relates to other metrics). This applies to ALL models, ALL projects, ALL future metrics.

log_likelihood.title: Log-Likelihood
log_likelihood.description: How well the model explains the observed data. Higher means the model's learned states fit actual price patterns better.
log_likelihood.detects: Whether the model has found meaningful structure in the data vs. random noise. A model that can't explain the data will have low LL.
log_likelihood.purpose: The fundamental measure of model quality. If LL is low, nothing downstream (regimes, transitions, SHAP) can be trusted.
log_likelihood.usage: Watch the curve shape: rapid rise = learning, plateau = converged, declining = numerical issues. Compare final LL across runs — higher is better for the same dataset.
log_likelihood.crossMetrics: Converges WITH assignment_stability. If LL plateaus but stability is low, the model found structure but can't decide which bars belong where. If both plateau together, the model is confident and done.
log_likelihood.healthy: Plateaus = converged. Still rising = still learning.

assignment_stability.title: Assignment Stability
assignment_stability.description: What percentage of bars kept the same regime label between consecutive Gibbs iterations.
assignment_stability.detects: Convergence confidence. When the sampler stops changing its mind about which regime each bar belongs to, training is done.
assignment_stability.purpose: The single best convergence indicator. More reliable than log-likelihood because it measures what you actually care about — are the regime assignments settled?
assignment_stability.usage: Watch for it to cross 95%. Below 90% = still exploring. 90-95% = close but some ambiguous bars. Above 95% = converged. If it never reaches 95%, some bars genuinely sit between two regimes.
assignment_stability.crossMetrics: Should rise together with log_likelihood. If stability is high but num_regimes keeps changing, the model is stable within each K but hasn't settled on how many regimes to use. Pair with switch_rate — high stability + low switch_rate = clean, tradeable regimes.
assignment_stability.healthy: Target >95%. Oscillation means some bars are ambiguous between states.

silhouette_score.title: Silhouette Score
silhouette_score.description: How similar each bar is to its assigned regime versus the nearest other regime. Range [-1, 1]. Higher means cleaner, more distinct clusters.
silhouette_score.detects: Whether regimes are genuinely separated in feature space or overlapping. Low silhouette means regimes bleed into each other.
silhouette_score.purpose: The gold-standard cluster quality metric. If silhouette is low, the model's regime distinctions may be arbitrary rather than reflecting real market structure.
silhouette_score.usage: Watch for it to stabilize above 0.30. Below 0.20 = regimes overlap significantly. Above 0.50 = excellent separation.
silhouette_score.crossMetrics: Compare with davies_bouldin (should be inverse). If silhouette is high but return_separation p-values are >0.05, regimes separate in feature space but not in returns — check feature selection.

calinski_harabasz.title: Calinski-Harabasz Index
calinski_harabasz.description: Ratio of between-cluster to within-cluster variance. Higher means tighter clusters that are farther apart.
calinski_harabasz.detects: Overall cluster compactness and separation. Scale-dependent, so compare across runs on the same data, not across different datasets.
calinski_harabasz.purpose: Complements silhouette — penalizes loose, overlapping clusters more aggressively. Good for detecting when regimes are 'smeared' across feature space.
calinski_harabasz.usage: Higher is better. Compare across runs with same data. Drops significantly if a noisy regime is added that doesn't capture real structure.
calinski_harabasz.crossMetrics: Tends to favor more clusters up to a point. If CH keeps rising as K increases, there may be genuine sub-structure. If it peaks and drops, that peak K is the natural number of regimes.

davies_bouldin.title: Davies-Bouldin Index
davies_bouldin.description: Average similarity between each cluster and its most similar cluster. Lower means less overlap between regimes.
davies_bouldin.detects: Which pairs of regimes are too similar. High DB means at least one pair of regimes is nearly indistinguishable.
davies_bouldin.purpose: Directly identifies redundant regimes. If DB > 1.5, the model has regimes that should be merged — reducing K would improve quality.
davies_bouldin.usage: Lower is better. Below 1.0 = good separation. Above 1.5 = significant overlap. Above 2.0 = regimes are barely distinguishable.
davies_bouldin.crossMetrics: Inverse of silhouette. If DB is high, check the emission heatmap for rows that look identical — those regimes should merge.

adjusted_rand_index.title: Adjusted Rand Index
adjusted_rand_index.description: Measures assignment stability between consecutive model state snapshots, adjusted for chance. 1.0 = identical assignments.
adjusted_rand_index.detects: Whether the model has settled on a consistent regime structure or is still rearranging assignments between snapshots.
adjusted_rand_index.purpose: More robust than raw assignment_stability because it's invariant to regime relabeling. Two runs that discover the same structure but number regimes differently will still show ARI = 1.0.
adjusted_rand_index.usage: Watch for convergence toward 1.0. Below 0.70 after burn-in = model hasn't settled. Above 0.85 = stable.
adjusted_rand_index.crossMetrics: Should converge alongside assignment_stability. If stability is high but ARI is low, regime labels are swapping (label switching problem) — the model is consistent but numbering changes.

ess.title: Effective Sample Size
ess.description: Number of effectively independent samples in the Gibbs chain. Accounts for autocorrelation between consecutive iterations.
ess.detects: Sampler efficiency. If ESS is 50 out of 500 iterations, 90% of compute was wasted on correlated samples. If ESS is 200, the sampler is exploring efficiently.
ess.purpose: Determines how much useful information your training run actually produced. Low ESS means the sampler is stuck and you need more iterations or different priors.
ess.usage: ESS / total_iterations > 0.20 is good. Below 0.10 = poor mixing — consider changing alpha or kappa.
ess.crossMetrics: Low ESS with high autocorrelation = sampler stuck. Low ESS with oscillating LL = multimodal posterior.

num_regimes.title: Active Regimes (K)
num_regimes.description: How many distinct market states the model discovered. The HDP prior lets the model create and kill regimes automatically — no fixed K.
num_regimes.detects: The natural number of market states in the data. The model births new regimes when existing ones can't explain a pattern, and kills regimes that become redundant.
num_regimes.purpose: Tells you the complexity of the market structure the model found. Too few regimes = the model is blind to important distinctions. Too many = it's hallucinating structure in noise.
num_regimes.usage: Should stabilize within the first 20% of iterations. If it keeps fluctuating, try increasing kappa (stickier) or decreasing alpha (fewer states). For forex, 3-8 regimes is typical. For futures, 5-15.
num_regimes.crossMetrics: Directly affects beta_entropy — more regimes = higher possible entropy. Watch num_regimes + self_transition together: if K is high but self_transition is low, you have too many noisy micro-regimes. If K is low but self_transition is very high, the model might be missing real structure.
num_regimes.healthy: Stable count = model settled on structure. 5-15 typical for forex.

mean_self_transition.title: Self-Transition Rate
mean_self_transition.description: How likely the model is to stay in the same regime on the next bar. Driven by kappa (sticky prior).
mean_self_transition.detects: Regime persistence — are the discovered states real market conditions that last multiple bars, or noise that flips every bar?
mean_self_transition.purpose: Directly determines if regimes are tradeable. You can't act on a regime that lasts 1-2 bars. Self-transition rate tells you the average regime duration before the model expects a switch.
mean_self_transition.usage: Higher = longer regime durations. At 1m bars: 50% = ~2 bar average hold, 80% = ~5 bar hold, 90% = ~10 bar hold. If too low, increase kappa. If too high, decrease kappa or the model only sees one dominant regime.
mean_self_transition.crossMetrics: Inverse of switch_rate (1 - self_transition ≈ switch_rate). Pair with avg_dwell for the actual bar count. If self_transition is high but avg_dwell is low, there's a mismatch — check for one dominant regime with many tiny regimes.
mean_self_transition.healthy: 50-80% healthy for 1m bars. Below 50% = noise. Above 90% = too sticky.

switch_rate.title: Switch Rate
switch_rate.description: Fraction of consecutive bars that change regime. Measures how often the model detects a state transition.
switch_rate.detects: Regime transition frequency — how choppy or smooth the regime assignments are. High switch rate = the model sees constant state changes.
switch_rate.purpose: Trading signal quality. Each regime switch is a potential trade signal. Too many switches = false signals. Too few = you miss real transitions. This metric tells you the signal-to-noise ratio of regime changes.
switch_rate.usage: Should decrease as the sampler converges (early iterations are noisy). Final value tells you expected trade frequency. At 30% on 1m bars = ~18 switches per hour = too noisy for most strategies. At 5% = ~3 switches per hour = actionable.
switch_rate.crossMetrics: Mirror of self_transition (switch_rate ≈ 1 - self_transition). Compare with avg_dwell — if switch_rate is 20% but avg_dwell is only 2 bars, transitions cluster in bursts rather than spreading evenly. Pair with assignment_stability — if stability is high but switch_rate is still high, the model confidently assigns rapid regime changes (real market chop).
switch_rate.healthy: 20-50% for 1m bars. Below 10% = over-sticky. Above 60% = noise.

avg_dwell.title: Avg Dwell Time
avg_dwell.description: Mean number of consecutive bars the model stays in one regime before switching. Longer dwell = more meaningful structure.
avg_dwell.detects: Regime duration — the average holding period of a market state. This is what determines if regimes are actionable for trading.
avg_dwell.purpose: The most direct measure of tradeability. If avg dwell is 2 bars at 1m, you have 2 minutes per regime — barely enough to enter and exit. At 10 bars, you have 10-minute windows to act on the regime signal.
avg_dwell.usage: Multiply by your timeframe to get real duration: 5 bars × 1m = 5 minutes per regime. For scalping strategies, 3-5 bars is enough. For swing strategies, you want 10+. If dwell is too short, increase kappa.
avg_dwell.crossMetrics: Directly computed from self_transition: avg_dwell ≈ 1/(1 - self_transition). But the actual value accounts for regime-specific persistence — some regimes may have 2-bar dwell while others have 20-bar. Compare with switch_rate for consistency. If avg_dwell is 5 but switch_rate is 40%, some regimes are much stickier than others.
avg_dwell.healthy: 2-5 bars at 1m. Higher at slower timeframes.

beta_entropy.title: Beta Entropy
beta_entropy.description: How evenly the model distributes bars across regimes. Controlled by gamma (concentration parameter).
beta_entropy.detects: Regime balance — whether all regimes are used meaningfully or if one regime dominates while others are nearly empty. High entropy = balanced usage.
beta_entropy.purpose: Identifies degenerate models. If one regime has 90% of bars and the rest split 10%, the model essentially found one state (useless). Healthy entropy means each regime captures a distinct, meaningful portion of the market.
beta_entropy.usage: Stable entropy = good. If it drops during training, regimes are consolidating (the model is killing weak regimes). If it spikes, the model is redistributing bars (instability). Compare the final value across runs — lower entropy with same K means more concentrated assignments.
beta_entropy.crossMetrics: Directly tied to num_regimes — more regimes allows higher maximum entropy. If K=10 but entropy is low, most regimes are empty shells. If K=3 and entropy is high, all three regimes are well-populated and distinct. Watch entropy + num_regimes together to distinguish 'found 3 strong regimes' from 'found 10 weak ones'.
beta_entropy.healthy: Stable is good. Dropping = regimes consolidating. Spiking = instability.

convergence_delta.title: Convergence Delta
convergence_delta.description: Change in log-likelihood between EM iterations. Measures how much the model is still learning per step.
convergence_delta.detects: Learning rate — whether each iteration is still improving the model or if it has converged. The EM algorithm guarantees this never goes negative (if it does, there's a numerical bug).
convergence_delta.purpose: Tells you when to stop training. Once delta drops below threshold, additional iterations waste compute without improving the model.
convergence_delta.usage: Starts large, decays toward zero. When it drops below 1e-6, the model is converged. If it oscillates instead of decaying, try more random restarts — the model may be stuck in a local optimum.
convergence_delta.crossMetrics: Leads log_likelihood — when delta approaches zero, LL has plateaued. If delta is near zero but assignment_stability is low, the EM converged to a bad optimum. Increase n_restarts.

mean_self_transition.title: Self-Transition Rate
mean_self_transition.description: Probability of staying in bull or bear state on the next bar.
mean_self_transition.detects: How persistent the two states are. In a 2-state model this directly determines the average length of bull and bear runs.
mean_self_transition.purpose: With only 2 states, this metric is especially important — it determines if the model found meaningful trend/counter-trend structure or just noise.
mean_self_transition.usage: For a useful 2-state model, you want 70-90%. Below 60% means the states flip too fast to be tradeable. Above 95% means the model barely switches — it found one dominant state.
mean_self_transition.crossMetrics: In a 2-state model, self_transition directly gives you the transition matrix (the off-diagonal is 1 - self_transition). Compare with log_likelihood — if LL is high but self_transition is near 50%, the model fits the data but doesn't find directional structure.
